summary: Last Signal is a bilingual (Arabic/English) interactive website that tells the story of 12 NASA spacecraft left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Each craft speaks in its own voice through five short chapters: Who am I? How did I work? What did I discover? Where am I now? and My last signal. Kids and casual space fans can tap a craft, read or listen to its story, take a short quiz and see how long it has been silent. The site connects each machine's engineering to the science it made possible, using facts from NASA mission pages and the NSSDCA archive. It answers the challenge by turning dense mission records into personal stories that make young people care about these robotic explorers.
details: What it does. Last Signal presents 12 craft: the Apollo 11 Eagle descent stage and the Lunar Roving Vehicles (Moon); Viking 1, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity (Mars); and NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer 10, Kepler, Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 (asteroid and deep space). Every craft has a first-person story with real dates, distances and discoveries, for example InSight's recorded marsquakes revealing Mars's liquid core, Ingenuity proving powered flight on another world, and NEAR Shoemaker landing on asteroid Eros although it was never designed to land. How it works. Visitors filter craft by Moon, Mars or deep space, search by name, filter by status (transmitting, silent, drifting, parked) and browse a timeline. Opening a craft shows its story, a NASA image with credit and caption, a live counter of the time since its last signal, a read-aloud button and a two-question quiz with points and ranks. The whole site is one HTML file that works in Arabic and English, right-to-left and left-to-right, and runs on phones. Benefits. It gives school-age and casual audiences a storytelling entry point to space history, keeps accuracy by linking every craft to its NASA source page, and is accessible: keyboard navigation, readable text, captions on images and audio narration. What we hope to achieve. To make these machines feel like characters, so young people connect with the engineering and the science behind them and feel inspired to explore further. Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, SVG illustrations, the browser's built-in speech synthesis for narration, and Netlify for hosting.
